headerBody: Italy: Tourist Scams maps the exact plays that work the queues at the Colosseum, the crush at the Trevi Fountain, the Grand Canal, and the alleys behind Napoli Centrale. Every entry is documented against Polizia di Stato and Carabinieri reporting, Guardia di Finanza counterfeit seizures, r/ItalyTravel threads, and verified Italian news — then drawn as a comic so you recognize the setup before it reaches the pitch.
quadHead: Four ways Italy works the queue, the crowd, and the canal.

quad.title: The Scippatori Moped Snatch
quad.tl: A two-rider Vespa accelerates past on Via Toledo and the passenger tears the bag or watch off you in one motion — one British tourist lost a €35,000 Rolex from his wrist in broad daylight.

quad.title: The Friendship-Bracelet Tie-On
quad.tl: “Your shoe's untied” — you glance down, a woven bracelet is knotted onto your wrist as a “gift,” and then it's €10–€20, with confederates closing in if you refuse.

quad.title: The Camorra Knock-Off Blanket
quad.tl: Fake Gucci, Fendi and Louis Vuitton spread on a blanket near Napoli Centrale — buying one is the crime, and a Dutch tourist was fined €2,900 on the spot for a single counterfeit Prada bag.

quad.title: Gondola Price Gouging
quad.tl: “€50, nice tour” turns into a 20-minute back-canal loop, then a higher bill — the city's fixed rate is €80 for 30 minutes (€100 after 7pm), only from licensed stations.

inside.head: Every scam, fully worked out — and the phrase that ends it.

body: Italy: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Italian police reporting — the Polizia di Stato (113) and Carabinieri (112) — Guardia di Finanza counterfeit seizures, r/ItalyTravel threads, and verified local news. Sourced and re-reported, not recycled from blog lists.

149 specific scams across Rome, Venice, Florence, Naples, Milan and 15 more cities — the costumed-centurion photo demand, the Trevi pickpocket crush, the Fiumicino flat-rate lie, the coperto pad, the scippatori moped snatch. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Italian phrases that shut them down, written phonetically so you can show them on your phone.
Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched every year, and the current edition sits in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Italy relaxed, not braced.
